new_statements.quote: Bartholomew (1980) argumenta que el pochuteco sufrió un cambio del patrón acentual debido a influencia del chatino. Ella señala que en variantes conservadoras que preserven las vocales átonas las lenguas chatinas tienen acento en la última sílaba de raíces mientras que lenguas zapotecas tienen el acento en la primera. Probablemente tiene razón que la influencia es de chatino, aunque debemos notar que lenguas zapotecas que han elidido vocales postónicas ahora tienen un patrón acentual yámbico (Arellanes 2015). Esto lo podemos ver en préstamos y compuestos: [...]
new_statements.translation: Bartholomew (1980) argues that Pochutec underwent a change of stress pattern due to Chatino influence. She points out that, in conservative varieties that preserve the unstressed vowels, the Chatino languages have stress on the last syllable of roots whereas Zapotec languages have stress on the first. She is probably right that the influence is from Chatino, although we must note that Zapotec languages that have elided post-tonic vowels now have an iambic stress pattern (Arellanes 2015). We can see this in loans and compounds: [...]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Family/area-level only: Zapotec stress is root stress, on the first root syllable where post-tonic vowels survive; Southern-Zapotec-area languages, Cisyautepecan (Dí'tsèh, to which Beam de Azcona assigns Lapaguía and Guivini) included, lost post-tonic vowels so native roots are mostly monosyllabic and stressed, and polysyllables (Spanish loans, compounds) are stressed iambically/finally, with unstressed syllables lacking tonal contrasts (Beam de Azcona 2014: 655). No source states the rule for Lapaguía-Guivini itself.
new_statements.exceptions: Loans and compounds are the polysyllabic cases (iambic pattern); otherwise none — the statement is not about this language specifically.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about 'lenguas zapotecas' generally and Southern Zapotec languages with post-tonic vowel loss; its application to lapa1249 rests only on Beam de Azcona's classification of Lapaguía(-Guivini) as a variety of the Cisyautepecan Dí'tsèh continuum (SAIL 2019 slides p.8; INALI 2018 handout p.27). Word-level (root) stress; tonal languages. Not a language-specific description, hence low confidence and not catalog-eligible.
new_statements.identity_note: ISO ztl / lapa1249 = Zapotec of Santiago Lapaguía, San Juan Guivini, La Merced del Potrero and San Felipe Lachilló (SE of Miahuatlán, Oaxaca). INALI (2008) files Santiago Lapaguía and San Juan Guivini under <zapoteco de la costa este> (together with San Miguel del Puerto localities and Santa María Xadani = xada1235), while San Bartolo Lapaguía (a different town) is <zapoteco de la Sierra sur, del norte>. Beam de Azcona (2004, 2018, 2019) treats Lapaguía and Guivini as varieties of the Cisyautepecan 'Dí'tsèh' dialect continuum (with Quiegolani quie?, Quioquitani-Quierí quio1241, San Juan/San Pedro Mixtepec mixt1426, Xanaguía, Xanica sant1451/1452), and argues (INALI 2018 handout p.27) it should not be counted as a language distinct from the rest of Dí'tsèh. Glottolog's alternative name 'Zapoteco de Asunción Tlacolulita' for lapa1249 looks like a mis-mapping (Tlacolulita is zpk/asun? a separate Transyautepecan language per Beam de Azcona). The stress statement quoted is family/area-level (Zapotec; Southern Zapotec area), not a description of this variety.

sources.note: pp.4-5 §2.1.2: Zapotec languages (conservative varieties) stress the first syllable of roots, Chatino the last; Zapotec languages that elided post-tonic vowels now have an iambic stress pattern visible in loans and compounds (Arellanes 2015). Family-level statement, not specific to Lapaguía-Guivini.

sources.citation: Beam de Azcona, Rosemary G. 2014. Algunos rasgos lingüísticos del zapoteco sureño. In R. Barriga Villanueva & E. Herrera Zendejas (eds.), Lenguas, estructuras y hablantes: estudios en homenaje a Thomas C. Smith Stark, vol. 2. México: El Colegio de México (author's scan; scanned here with tesseract-spa, 300 dpi).
sources.note: Group-level only (p.655, scanned noisy): in Southern Zapotec unstressed vowels were lost historically; new unstressed syllables arise in Spanish loans and compounds and 'difieren de las sílabas tónicas por su falta de contrastes tonales'; monosyllabicity is strong in Macro-Coatecan, Miahuatecan and Cisyautepecan languages. No Lapaguía/Guivini data. Bibliography cites Méndez Espinosa 2004 (CIESAS thesis on Cisyautepecan dialectology).
sources.venue: Lenguas, estructuras y hablantes: estudios en homenaje a Thomas C

sources.citation: Beam de Azcona, Rosemary G. 2019. Southern Zapotec verb classes. Amerindia 41: 121-165.
sources.note: Nothing on stress; uses 'Guivini' verb-class data (Table 14 'Quiegolani, Guivini'; p.152 'easternmost varieties, Quiegolani and Guivini'); p.138 says all Cisyautepecan data are taken from cited sources (Antonio Ramos 2015, Black 1994, Hopkins 1995, Hunn et al. n.d., Méndez 2004, Olive 1995, Piper 1995, Ward 1987) — by elimination the Guivini data come from Méndez Espinosa 2004.

sources.citation: Beam de Azcona, Rosemary G. 2019. The Southern Zapotec linguistic area and the case of Dítsèh (Cisyautepecan), a Central Zapotec language of the Sierra Sur. Slides, Symposium on American Indian Languages, University of Arizona.
sources.note: Nothing on stress; p.8 lists Lapaguía among 'Documented varieties of Cisyautepecan' (Quierí, Quioquitani, San Pedro Mixtepec, San Juan Mixtepec, Xanaguía, Xanica, Leapi, Lachivigoza, Quiegolani, Lapaguía), i.e. treats it as part of the Dítsèh dialect continuum.

sources.note: Nothing on stress; p.27: INALI's <zapoteco de la costa este> (ditsa') = San Juan Guivini, Santiago Lapaguía, San Miguel del Puerto localities, Santa María Xadani, San Felipe Lachilló; 'los informantes de Méndez (2004) de Quierí y Mixtepec mencionaron a Lapaguía y Guivini como pueblos cuya habla era inteligible para ellos. Por ende esta variante no se debe considerar como una lengua distinta al resto del dí’tsèh.'
